title: Equilibrium sampling computers operating near thermal energy per sample

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a programmable physical computer that uses thermal fluctuations and relaxation toward equilibrium to draw samples from a probability distribution specified by its user. Instead of calculating every random update through digital instructions, the device would encode the desired distribution in a programmable energy function and let its physical dynamics perform the sampling. The breakthrough would be an end-to-end demonstration of accurate sampling with total measured energy per effectively independent output approaching the thermal energy scale kT, while substantially outperforming a strong digital implementation of the same workload.

An internal stochastic update, a Gibbs iteration, and an independent output sample are different units of work. Successive device states can remain strongly correlated, so many updates may be needed to obtain the information carried by one independent sample. The proposed capability therefore concerns useful output after accounting for equilibration, correlations, programming and readout. A large collection of probabilistic bits, a sparse Ising sampler, or an estimated energy cost for an internal update would be a component toward this capability, rather than its completed demonstration.

significance.text: Sampling is an important computational primitive in statistical inference, optimization and generative modeling. A system that could physically produce sufficiently accurate independent samples at total measured energy near kT would establish an exceptionally efficient native primitive for probabilistic computation. The supplied compilation paper gives this prospect a concrete technical basis by describing how stochastic programs can be translated into thermodynamic sampling kernels and demonstrating applications in software.

The direct benefit would be lower energy consumption for the sampling workloads on which an advantage was actually measured. Broader benefits to inference systems, optimization pipelines or generative models would depend on how much of each application can use the sampler, how accurately its target distribution can be represented, how quickly it mixes, and how much energy the surrounding system consumes. The supplied evidence does not quantify a general digital energy cost per effective sample or establish automatic gains across AI workloads.

Conceptual synthesis: near-kT sampling should not be equated with general-purpose digital computation near the Landauer scale. Sampling produces stochastic outputs with a specified distribution; deterministic logic must preserve specified logical behavior, and the Landauer bound concerns logically irreversible information erasure. Here, kT is the proposed energy scale for evaluating useful sampling output, not a source-established universal minimum energy per sample. A successful sampler would establish a distinct computational capability without by itself demonstrating equally efficient deterministic computing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied evidence is a measured device demonstration that samples a user-specified distribution on a workload also runnable digitally, produces outputs of verified quality, and achieves both near-thermal total energy per independent sample and a large matched advantage over a strong digital baseline. The available paper supplies software demonstrations and hardware energy estimates; the vendor article supplies specifications and deployment plans. Together they do not establish this end-to-end result, although they also do not establish that no such result exists elsewhere.

A central scientific and algorithmic barrier is making programmable equilibrium dynamics yield the intended distribution accurately and quickly enough to be useful. A target distribution must be represented within the hardware's available interactions and parameters, with compilation and approximation errors controlled. Relaxation toward equilibrium must then be distinguished from adequate exploration of the target: slow mixing and correlations can make a low energy cost per iteration coexist with a high energy cost per effective independent sample. These issues require workload-specific evidence.

The engineering barrier is preserving an advantage across the complete computation. Programming, initialization, equilibration, readout and required host processing must be included under a declared accounting boundary. The paper distinguishes sampling iterations from programming and readout operations, making these costs material to interpreting its energy estimates. Proposed engineering requirements include measuring those contributions, controlling distribution errors as devices scale, and showing that any amortization of setup costs corresponds to a practical workload rather than an artificially favorable accounting choice.

current_state.text: Amico et al., Thermalizing Stochastic Programs, arXiv:2608.01615v2, is an August 2026 preprint describing compilation onto thermodynamic sampling hardware. Its inspected text explicitly states that all demonstrations were executed in software. It therefore supports a compilation framework and software application demonstrations, rather than a measured hardware demonstration of near-kT sampling. The supplied review identifies both Ashwin Gopal and Guillaume Verdon among the authors, correcting their omission from the earlier author enumeration. The version header and body give different August dates, so the month is the reliable date resolution available here.

The preprint estimates approximately 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ J per Gibbs iteration for a chip of about 250,000 nodes. Dividing those figures gives approximately 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ J per node per iteration. At an assumed physical temperature of 300 K, that is about 2.9 × 10⁵ kT per node per iteration. The operating temperature is not specified in the supplied evidence, and this illustrative normalization is neither measured device energy nor energy per independent sample. The retained paper extraction is truncated during Section IV.5; Appendix B's advertised energy breakdown was unavailable to the review, limiting assessment of the estimate's full accounting assumptions.

Extropic's supplied article specifies a Z1 die with eight cores, 269,568 probabilistic bits, 215,904 coupling parameters, a sampling rate above 50 MHz and power below 1 W. These are vendor statements. The article describes Z1 as taped out and early access as planned for 2027; it does not establish broad availability or an independently measured workload result. Its stated sampling rate does not establish a rate of independent output samples. The retained article was complete, but its text displays Summer 2026 and does not confirm the earlier attribution to 29 October 2026.

Evidence boundary: the supplied materials do not establish a qualifying independent audit, and the empty freshness record prevents a bounded conclusion about the field as of 1 November 2026. The source attributed in the earlier research to Korbel and coauthors, arXiv:2604.26601v1, has no captured text in the supplied source index. Its identity, characterization of computation as an emerging application, and relevance to thermal-scale computing therefore remain unverified here. These access limitations leave questions open; they are not evidence that the underlying claims or results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance test: an independent third party should evaluate at least one sampling task and one combinatorial inference task that both the physical device and a digital implementation can execute. Target accuracy, solution quality, convergence checks and the method for estimating effective sample size should be specified before evaluation. For the inference task, evaluation should establish that the returned distribution or inferred quantities meet the stated target, rather than relying only on favorable individual solutions. Passing these tests would establish demonstrated breadth on those benchmarks, not universal sampling ability or general-purpose superiority.
completion_criteria.label: Independent evaluation verifies sampling and inference meet prespecified targets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed numerical thresholds are total measured energy below 100 kT per effective independent sample at the device's physical operating temperature, together with at least a 1,000-fold energy advantage over a strong same-year GPU or CPU baseline at matched output quality. Both thresholds are choices for this innovation record, not established scientific standards. The baseline should use an appropriate, well-tuned digital algorithm under comparable task conditions, with the hardware, software and measurement boundaries disclosed.
completion_criteria.label: Below 100 kT per effective independent sample; 1,000-fold matched-quality digital energy advantage

completion_criteria.text: The proposed energy account should include initialization, programming, equilibration, readout and required host overhead, with an explicit policy for amortizing setup costs over samples and repeated uses. Evaluation should distinguish internal update rate from effective independent sample throughput and report latency, sustained throughput and accuracy alongside energy. It should also disclose the target representation, interaction constraints, problem sizes and conditions under which the demonstrated advantage holds.
completion_criteria.label: Report full resource costs, sampling performance, and demonstrated operating limits

completion_criteria.text: For reproducibility, the proposed demonstration should publish raw power traces, timing records, sample sequences, target distributions or reproducible problem generators, compilation settings, baseline code and the effective-sample-size method. Repeated runs and independent reproduction should test whether the claimed accuracy and energy advantage persist. These requirements operationalize the sampling goal and the programming/readout distinctions documented in the paper, but the acceptance protocol itself is a proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Publish reproducibility artifacts and independently reproduce accuracy and energy advantage

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: THR-03, General-purpose digital computation near the Landauer scale, is the closest neighboring entry. Both concern energy-efficient information processing, but THR-08 targets independent samples from programmed probability distributions, whereas THR-03's title identifies general-purpose digital computation near an erasure-related energy scale. Only THR-03's title was supplied, so a more precise boundary between the two records cannot be verified.

Conceptual overlap: probabilistic computing, statistical inference and computer architecture supply the immediate computational context for THR-08. Probabilistic bits provide stochastic components; compilation maps programs or distributions onto their interactions; architecture determines how programming, sampling, readout and host computation fit together. None of these components alone establishes the proposed total energy per independent output.

Roster-based comparison: THR-01, a computable thermodynamic potential for far-from-equilibrium continuum transport, THR-11, operational temperature and entropy for far-from-equilibrium matter, and THR-12, predictive thermodynamic design of far-from-equilibrium chemical reaction networks, share concerns about thermodynamic description or design. Their titles identify different central targets from THR-08's programmed equilibrium sampling and measured computational output. This comparison does not imply that those theories are prerequisites for the sampler.

Roster-based comparison: THR-02 addresses the combined efficiency, power and steadiness of useful heat engines; THR-04 addresses heat–charge decoupling for solid-state conversion; THR-06 addresses non-thermal carriers in solar conversion; and THR-07 addresses synthetic chemomechanical engines. These entries concern useful energy conversion or mechanical work, whereas THR-08 evaluates the energy cost of a probabilistic information-processing output. Their performance goals should not be treated as interchangeable.

Roster-based comparison: THR-05 seeks a size-extensive quantum advantage in thermodynamic performance, while the supplied THR-08 concept does not require a quantum mechanism. THR-09 concerns predictive thermodynamic design of self-replicators, and THR-10 concerns a laboratory measurement of the Unruh temperature. Neither self-replication nor an Unruh-temperature measurement is part of the proposed sampling demonstration. These remain separate innovations despite their common thermodynamic setting.

unresolved_issues: Whether an independently audited device demonstration meeting these proposed criteria existed as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved; no bounded freshness search record was supplied.
The preprint's complete energy breakdown, including Appendix B, was unavailable in the truncated extraction.
The physical operating temperature, full system boundary and relationship between the estimated Gibbs-iteration cost and effective independent sample cost remain unspecified in the supplied evidence.
Z1's vendor specifications do not resolve measured workload accuracy, effective independent sample throughput, total energy accounting or performance against a matched digital baseline.
The exact date of the Extropic article remains unresolved beyond its displayed Summer 2026 label; the earlier 29 October attribution is unconfirmed.
The identity and substantive claims of the source attributed to Korbel and coauthors cannot be verified without its missing captured text.
The proposed acceptance protocol still needs concrete workloads, accuracy targets, an effective-sample-size procedure and an amortization policy before it can be executed.
Only titles were supplied for neighboring roster entries, limiting precise overlap analysis, especially with THR-03.
